title: 1992 AHSME Problem 21
statement: For a finite sequence \(A=(a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n)\) of numbers, the Cesàro sum of \(A\) is defined to be \[ \frac{S_1+S_2+\cdots+S_n}{n}, \] where \[ \begin{aligned} S_k&=a_1+a_2+a_3+\cdots+a_k\\ &\qquad(1\le k\le n). \end{aligned} \] If the Cesàro sum of the \(99\)-term sequence \((a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_{99})\) is \(1000,\) what is the Cesàro sum of the \(100\)-term sequence \((1,a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_{99})?\)

solutions.text:
The given condition says \(S_1+\cdots+S_{99}=99{,}000.\) For the new sequence, the partial sums are \(1,1+S_1,\ldots,1+S_{99}.\) Their sum is \[ 100+(S_1+\cdots+S_{99})=99{,}100. \] Dividing by \(100\) gives the new Cesàro sum \(991.\)

Thus the correct answer is A.
hints: Convert the first Cesàro sum into the value of \(S_1+\cdots+S_{99}\)
Each new partial sum is \(1\) plus an old partial sum, with one initial partial sum equal to \(1\)
